articles.title: Amazon CloudWatch announces log routing and chained log parsers
articles.overview: Amazon CloudWatch now supports conditional log routing and chained parsers via pipelines, giving you more control over how log data is transformed and which CloudWatch log group it's sent to.
articles.explanation: CloudWatch pipelines is a fully managed service that ingests, transforms, and routes telemetry to CloudWatch without managing infrastructure. Log pipelines often carry a mix of event types that belong in different places, and individual events can nest one log format inside another. With conditional log routing, you define routes that send each event to a different CloudWatch log group based on conditions evaluated against processed fields, so you can separate events by severity, source, or type and apply the right retention and access controls to each. With chained parsers, you can apply multiple parser processors in sequence, where later parsers consume fields produced by earlier ones. For example, you can parse a JSON envelope first, then apply a Grok parser to a field it extracts. Together, these capabilities let you structure diverse log formats and route them to the right log groups in a single pipeline.

articles.overview: Amazon CloudFront now supports end-to-end IPv6 delivery to origins inside your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), with the new dual-stack VPC origins.

Customers faced a tradeoff: move origins to public subnets for IPv6 and give up VPC origin security or keep them private and stay on IPv4. articles.title: Amazon DynamoDB Streams now supports timestamp-based stream processing
articles.overview: Amazon DynamoDB Streams now supports timestamp-based stream processing, enabling you to begin reading stream records from a specific point in time.
articles.explanation: Previously, you could only start from the oldest retained record (up to 24 hours old) or from new records written after you start consuming the stream. Now, you can supply a timestamp and begin processing at the first record written at or after that time using the AT_TIMESTAMP shard iterator type. Timestamp-based stream processing can be used with the Amazon Kinesis Client Library (KCL) through the DynamoDB Streams Kinesis adapter. It helps you avoid reprocessing entire retained streams or missing records when resuming stream consumption, supporting common use cases such as recovery after an interruption, data replay for debugging and auditing by reading from a specific point in the past, skipping a backlog by resuming from a recent timestamp near the latest records, and synchronizing after a restore by beginning at the export timestamp following a point-in-time recovery (PITR) export. Timestamp-based stream processing is available in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. There is no additional charge for this feature beyond standard GetRecords API request charges.

The Q6_V_vmux_QVV select keeps the scalar reference's x > 20 guard (ggml_compute_softplus_f32 in ggml-impl.h), which is what makes the vector path match the CPU result. articles.overview: Hi HN!
articles.explanation: Fakeipedia is an automatic world-building platform which takes an imagined world and makes a whole wiki that you can endlessly explore by clicking red links. articles.title: Amazon Braket now in scope for FedRAMP Class C
articles.overview: Amazon Braket is now in scope for FedRAMP Class C in AWS US Regions where Braket is available.
articles.explanation: The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) is a US government-wide program that delivers a standard approach to the security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring of cloud products and services. With FedRAMP Class C authorization, government customers and the organizations that serve them can use Amazon Braket to explore quantum computing within an authorized boundary. The AWS-operated components of Braket, including the API and SDK, job orchestration and management, compilation, and result storage in Amazon S3, are within the FedRAMP-certified boundary, while quantum workloads execute on third-party Quantum Hardware Providers (QHPs) outside that boundary. All data sent to QHPs meets AWS' privacy and security requirements including removal of all personally identifiable information, data encryption in transit and at rest, and adherence to AWS' standard data retention and deletion policies. To learn more about FedRAMP, visit AWS FedRAMP services and the FedRAMP Marketplace. To learn more about Amazon Braket, visit the Braket product page and Getting Started on Braket resources.

articles.explanation: Attention interleaves four sliding layers at a 513 window with one full layer. The sliding layers rotate with NeoX RoPE, the full layers are NoPE. GQA runs 48 query heads against 4 KV heads at head_dim 128 with a QK-RMSNorm, and every block carries four RMSNorms, so the attention and the MLP output are normalized before they rejoin the residual stream. Routing picks the experts from logits + expert_bias and weights them with the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, without renorm. The released FP8 checkpoint needs no special code, it goes through the generic weight_scale_inv path.

articles.title: b11730: cuda: cap MMQ Stream-K blocks at available work (#30553)
articles.overview: cuda: cap Stream-K blocks at the number of k-blocks Stream-K normally launches one CUDA block per SM.
articles.explanation: For small matrices, this can exceed the total number of output-tile/k-block pairs, leaving blocks with no work and adding launch and fixup overhead. Cap the grid at that count to remove these excess blocks without changing the useful rounded K ranges or numerical results. Assisted-by: Codex cuda: cap Stream-K blocks at the number of k iterations Cap the grid at the number of K_vram iterations across all output tiles, rounding up partial iterations. This removes extra CUDA blocks left by the k-block cap. Partial iterations can change FP32 summation grouping. MUL_MAT and MUL_MAT_ID backend tests pass on RTX 5090.

articles.title: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
articles.overview: I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-meta-and-i-never-felt-share-7517317918666211328-7C8N > I'm an engineer at Meta and I nev...
articles.explanation: I'm writing code these days and it all feels like a black box. This new standard of shipping with AI is moving so fast that if we're going to spend our time checking each line of code, it's going to take forever. That means you can end up with systems you've built where you don't truly understand how all the code works. You understand the high level, but not every detail. And maybe this is becoming the new standard. It goes against every instinct of being a software engineer.
